beats.headline: Stop building custom state machines.
beats.subline: Status tables and cron jobs are fragile. Durable execution is the fix.
beats.narration: Stop building custom status tables and Kafka-based state machines for long-running processes. You're just reinventing a distributed system that will eventually leak state or double-fire during a deployment.

beats.title: Patchwork vs. Durable Code

top.label: Manual Orchestration

bottom.label: Temporal Workflow

beats.narration: Temporal replaces scattered status tables with durable Java code. Your workflow logic resides in standard methods, and the engine handles persistence, retries, and timers for you.

beats.title: Temporal Architecture

nodes.label: Temporal Cluster
nodes.detail: Stores event logs and manages task queues

nodes.label: Task Queue
nodes.detail: gRPC long-polling bridge between cluster and worker

beats.narration: The Temporal Cluster never runs your code. It stores the event history. Your Java Workers poll the Task Queues via gRPC to execute the actual business logic.

beats.headline: Why your workflow code must be deterministic.
beats.subline: One call to Instant.now() can crash your entire production workflow.
beats.narration: Temporal doesn't save your thread stack. It saves an event history. If your code isn't deterministic, the replay will fail, and your workflow will crash.

beats.title: The Replay Mechanism

nodes.label: Event History
nodes.detail: Immutable log of past activity results

beats.narration: When a worker restarts, it replays the workflow from the start. For every activity completed in history, the SDK returns the cached result instead of re-running the I/O.

beats.title: Deterministic vs. Non-Deterministic
beats.narration: Never use Instant dot now or random UUIDs in your workflow. Use the Temporal SDK wrappers, which pull values from the event history to ensure consistency.

beats.title: Golden Rules for Workflows

steps.explanation: Database state changes over time. Always wrap I/O in an activity.
Standard logs duplicate on replay. Use the workflow-aware logger.

beats.narration: Follow these rules. If you perform I/O or non-deterministic logic in your workflow, you break the replay contract. Keep the workflow pure and push side effects into activities.

beats.headline: What happens when your API fails?
beats.subline: Stop writing manual retry loops. Use declarative activity options and Sagas.
beats.narration: Downstream APIs will fail. Instead of writing manual retry loops with exponential backoff, define your retry policy declaratively in your workflow code.

beats.title: Declarative Retries

steps.explanation: Exponential backoff is built-in. No more custom sleep loops.
Fail fast on business errors like declined cards.

beats.narration: Define your retry policy once. Temporal handles the scheduling, backoff, and state persistence automatically. If an error is non-retryable, the workflow catches it immediately.

beats.title: Saga Pattern for Rollbacks
beats.narration: Use the Saga helper to manage compensations. If a step fails, the saga runs the registered rollbacks in reverse order. Even the rollback itself is a retriable activity.

beats.title: Saga Lifecycle
beats.narration: The Saga pattern ensures your distributed transaction eventually reaches a consistent state, even if the rollback itself experiences transient network issues.

beats.headline: How to update code without breaking history.
beats.subline: Long-running workflows don't stop for your deployments. Here is how to evolve them safely.
beats.narration: What happens when you deploy new code while a workflow is waiting for a five-day timer? You risk a NonDeterministicException. Here is how to handle evolution.

beats.title: Signals & Queries

steps.explanation: Asynchronously update a running workflow's state.
Synchronously inspect workflow state without mutating it.

beats.narration: Signals allow external systems to influence a running workflow. Queries provide a read-only view into the workflow's internal state. Both are essential for long-running processes.

beats.title: Safe Evolution

steps.explanation: Records a version marker in history for new executions.
Old workflows skip the new code, new ones execute it.

beats.narration: Use getVersion to safely introduce code changes. It records a marker in the event history, ensuring old workflows don't try to execute logic they weren't designed for.

beats.title: Continue-As-New

lines.text: # Prevent history bloat for infinite loops

beats.narration: For infinite processes like billing cycles, use continue-as-new. It closes the current history and starts a fresh one, keeping your event logs small and performant.
